title: THEY PUT BRACKETS AROUND HER STORY… BUT DID SOMEONE TRY TO REMOVE THE MERCY OF JESUS?
paragraphs: THEY PUT BRACKETS AROUND HER STORY… BUT DID SOMEONE TRY TO REMOVE THE MERCY OF JESUS?

Why John 7:53–8:11 is missing from some ancient manuscripts, why modern Bibles warn readers about it, and what the woman caught in adultery can teach us about truth, grace, repentance, and the Savior who refuses to leave sinners unchanged.
Imagine opening your Bible to one of the most unforgettable encounters ever associated with Jesus Christ.
A woman is standing in the middle of an angry crowd.
Her shame has become public entertainment.
Her accusers are holding the Law over her head.
Death is being discussed as though her life means nothing.
And Jesus is there.
Then you notice something strange.
There are brackets around the entire story.
Or perhaps a footnote beneath the passage says:
“The earliest manuscripts do not include John 7:53–8:11.”
Wait.
What?
One of the most beloved accounts of mercy in the Bible comes with a warning that it may not have been part of John's original Gospel?
Was something removed?
Did someone tamper with Scripture?
Are modern Bible translators trying to erase the compassion of Jesus?
Or is there something much deeper happening here—something every Christian who truly loves the Word of God needs to understand?
Because this is not merely a question about eleven verses.
It is a question about whether we love the Bible enough to examine its history honestly.
Whether our faith can withstand difficult evidence.
And whether we are willing to distinguish what we desperately want a passage to say from what the evidence actually allows us to claim.
But there is another question hiding beneath the controversy.
If you had been standing in that courtyard, watching a terrified woman surrounded by people ready to condemn her, whose face would you have recognized?
The woman's?
The accusers'?
Or perhaps both?
Stay with me.
Because before we reach the end, we are going to confront something far more personal than brackets on a printed page.
We are going to confront the frightening possibility that we can defend the Bible with our mouths while resisting the very grace and holiness it reveals.
And that should make every one of us examine our hearts.
The passage traditionally known as the woman caught in adultery is found in John 7:53–8:11. Scholars often call it the Pericope Adulterae, meaning the passage about the adulterous woman.
The story begins with Jesus teaching in the temple.
Religious leaders bring before Him a woman who has allegedly been caught committing adultery.
They place her in the center of the gathering.
Not privately.
Not gently.
In front of everyone.
Then they challenge Jesus.
The King James Version records their accusation:
“Now Moses in the law commanded us, that such should be stoned: but what sayest thou?” (John 8:5, KJV).
The text immediately explains that their question was a trap. They were seeking grounds to accuse Jesus.
And that detail matters.
Because the woman is not the only person being examined in this encounter.
Jesus Himself is being tested.
The accusers appear to be interested in justice, but the narrative exposes their ulterior motive.
They want to use this woman's situation against Him.
Notice something else.
Where is the man?
The Law of Moses addressed both parties involved in adultery. Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22 make that clear.
Yet the account presents only the woman.
We are not told what happened to the man, whether he escaped, or why he was absent. We should not invent details Scripture does not provide.
But we can recognize the troubling imbalance in the scene.
One person stands exposed.
Others stand ready to condemn.
And Jesus refuses to be manipulated.
Then comes one of the most mysterious moments in the entire account.
Jesus bends down and writes on the ground.
What did He write?
The names of the accusers?
Their hidden sins?
A passage from the Law?
Perhaps a reference to Jeremiah 17:13, where those who forsake the Lord are associated with writing in the earth?
These interpretations have been suggested across Christian history.
But the passage does not tell us what Jesus wrote.
And sometimes faithfulness to Scripture means having the humility to say, “We do not know.”
The Greek verb used for His writing is κατέγραφεν (kategraphen), from katagraphō, meaning to write down or inscribe.
It does not reveal the content of His writing.
Whatever Jesus wrote, the narrative directs our attention toward what He said.
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.” (John 8:7, KJV).
The Greek reads:
Ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν πρῶτος ἐπ᾽ αὐτὴν βαλέτω λίθον.
Ho anamartētos hymōn prōtos ep’ autēn baletō lithon.
A close rendering is:
“Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.”
Consider the force of that moment.
Jesus does not declare adultery righteous.
He does not pretend the Law is meaningless.
He exposes the moral seriousness of those who are eager to carry out judgment while standing under judgment themselves.
The passage should not be twisted into the claim that no human court may ever punish wrongdoing or that Christians must never exercise moral discernment.
Its setting is a hostile attempt to trap Jesus through a public accusation.
His response exposes the accusers and their motives.
And then the stones begin to lose their power.
One by one, the accusers leave.
The woman remains.
Jesus asks whether anyone has condemned her.
She answers that no one has.
And He says:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV).
Read that again.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
But do not stop there.
“Go, and sin no more.”
Mercy.
And a summons to holiness.
Compassion.
And a call to change.
This is why so many believers treasure this account.
Yet now we must face the difficult historical question.
Why do modern Bibles place brackets around it?
The answer is not that translators suddenly decided they disliked the story.
It is not evidence of a secret campaign to erase Jesus' mercy.
And it is not proof that modern Christianity has abandoned the Bible.
The brackets exist because of a genuine textual question.
The New Testament was originally written in Greek, and we do not possess the original handwritten manuscripts produced by its authors.
What we have are thousands of Greek manuscripts and additional ancient translations, quotations, and other witnesses.
These manuscripts were copied across centuries.
Most textual differences are small—spelling variations, word order, or other changes that do not substantially alter meaning.
Some differences, however, concern larger passages.
John 7:53–8:11 is one of the most important examples.

Two of the earliest substantial surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel, Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus, both dating to the fourth century, do not contain this account in its familiar location.
Other early Greek witnesses also omit it.
The surviving manuscript evidence is not uniform, however.
The passage appears in many later Greek manuscripts and became deeply established in the Christian tradition.
And here is a particularly important detail.
In some manuscript traditions, this story appears in different locations.
Some witnesses place it elsewhere in John.
Others associate it with Luke, including a location after Luke 21:38.
That movement is significant.
When a passage appears in different positions across manuscript traditions, it can suggest that scribes were preserving a story whose placement in the Gospel text was uncertain.
This does not automatically tell us who first told the story.
It does not prove that the events never happened.
But it is important evidence when asking whether the passage originally stood where we now read it.

The earliest surviving Greek manuscript evidence and the passage's variable placement are major reasons why many textual scholars conclude that John 7:53–8:11 was probably not part of the original composition of the Fourth Gospel.
That is a serious conclusion.
And Christians should not be afraid to understand it.
Because loving Scripture does not require pretending that difficult manuscript evidence does not exist.
It requires handling that evidence truthfully.
Now consider another important witness.
The fourth-century Christian writer Didymus the Blind appears to refer to a story about a woman accused of sin before Jesus, although the details and textual relationship require caution.

And Augustine, writing in the late fourth and early fifth centuries, discussed the account and suggested that some people had removed it from their copies because they feared it might encourage adultery.
Augustine's observation is historically fascinating.
It shows that the passage was known and that its transmission was already being discussed in antiquity.
But we must be careful.
Augustine's explanation for why some copies lacked the story is not, by itself, proof that the passage originally belonged to John and was subsequently removed.
A historical explanation offered by an ancient writer is evidence of what that writer believed, not automatic confirmation of the events he proposed.
This distinction matters.
We should not replace one unsupported conspiracy with another merely because the second sounds more favorable to our expectations.
The evidence is complex.
And faithfulness requires honesty.
So what about the famous story itself?
Could Jesus actually have encountered this woman?
Could the event preserve an authentic memory from His ministry, even if it was not originally written by John?
Some scholars consider that possible.
Others are more skeptical.
The surviving evidence does not allow us to establish the episode's historicity with certainty.
That is why we should distinguish two questions that are often confused.
Did this account originally belong in the Gospel of John?
And did the event described actually happen?
Those are not identical questions.
A story could preserve an early historical memory without having been written by the author of the Gospel in which it later appeared.
But possibility is not proof.
Christians do not honor Jesus by claiming more certainty than the evidence supports.
And here is something many people miss.
The mercy of Jesus does not depend on the authenticity of this one disputed passage.
Even if John 7:53–8:11 was not part of John's original Gospel, the compassion, forgiveness, and transforming authority of Christ remain firmly established in undisputed New Testament passages.
Look at Luke 7:36–50.
A woman known as a sinner approaches Jesus in tears.
Others look at her with contempt.
Jesus speaks of forgiveness and faith.
Look at Luke 15.
Jesus tells of a father who welcomes his repentant, lost son.
Look at Luke 19:1–10.
Zacchaeus, a tax collector despised by many, encounters Jesus and responds with a transformed life.
Look at Mark 2:15–17.
Jesus shares a table with tax collectors and sinners, explaining that He came to call sinners.
Look at John 3:17.
God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world through Him might be saved.
And look at Romans 8:1.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV).
That truth does not hang on a disputed textual passage.
It stands on the Gospel itself.
But there is something even more important.
Jesus did not come merely to make guilty people feel better about remaining guilty.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to bear our sins.
He died and rose again.
The cross is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The cross reveals how seriously God takes sin—and how astonishingly far His love goes to redeem sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that we were innocent.
Not that our choices never mattered.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
But that Jesus Christ came to rescue people who could never rescue themselves.
Now return to the woman in the disputed passage.
Think about what makes this story so emotionally powerful.
She is standing in the center of a crowd.
Her failure is known.
Her future is uncertain.
The people surrounding her seem to know everything about her worst moment.
And nothing about her tears.
We are not told her name.
We are not told her family circumstances.
We are not told what happened to her afterward.
We are not even told whether she obeyed Jesus' final instruction.
And those silences should remain silences.
But perhaps the account unsettles us because we recognize something of ourselves in that courtyard.
Maybe your sin was never exposed publicly.
Maybe nobody gathered around you with stones.
Maybe your shame has never appeared on a screen, in a church meeting, or in a conversation behind your back.
But you know what it feels like to remember something you wish you could undo.
A relationship you damaged.
A betrayal you concealed.
A habit you promised God you would abandon.
A season when you knew the truth and still chose what was wrong.
Or perhaps you have been the person holding the stone.
You knew someone else's failure.
You repeated their story.
You enjoyed being right more than you desired their restoration.
You called it discernment.
But somewhere along the way, compassion disappeared.
And maybe the person who needs repentance today is not the one you have been judging.
Maybe it is you.
That is a hard thought.
I know.
Because it is easier to study a crowd from two thousand years ago than to recognize the crowd inside our own hearts.
It is easier to debate a textual footnote than to confess the bitterness we have been carrying.
It is easier to defend biblical authority online than to obey Christ when He tells us to forgive, repent, tell the truth, and love our enemies.
And that is where this discussion becomes painfully personal.
We can spend hours arguing about whether the woman caught in adultery belongs in John.
But what happens when the undisputed words of Jesus confront us?
What happens when He says, “Repent ye, and believe the gospel” (Mark 1:15)?
What happens when He tells us to forgive?
What happens when He calls us to deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him?
What happens when Scripture tells us that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9)?
Do we obey?
Or do we prefer arguments that never require surrender?
Please do not misunderstand.
Textual criticism matters.
Manuscript history matters.
Accurate translation matters.
If we believe Scripture is God's Word, then we should care deeply about what its authors actually wrote.
That is precisely why honest Bible translations alert readers to significant textual questions.
A footnote is not necessarily an attack on faith.
Sometimes it is an act of transparency.
A translator who quietly hides meaningful manuscript uncertainty may leave readers less informed.
A translator who identifies the uncertainty gives readers the opportunity to investigate the evidence.
And that is not something Christians need to fear.
The Greek word ἀλήθεια (alētheia) means truth.
In John 17:17, Jesus prays:
“Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.” (KJV).
The Greek phrase is:
ὁ λόγος ὁ σὸς ἀλήθειά ἐστιν
ho logos ho sos alētheia estin.
“Your word is truth.”
If we belong to the God of truth, we must not defend His Word with exaggerations, fabricated evidence, or claims we cannot substantiate.
Truth does not become more glorious when we decorate it with misinformation.
And faith does not become stronger by refusing to ask hard questions.
Some Christians will continue reading John 7:53–8:11 as part of their received biblical tradition.
Others will read it as an ancient account associated with Jesus while acknowledging that it probably was not part of John's original text.
Those differences deserve thoughtful discussion.
But neither position should become an excuse for contempt toward fellow believers.
The textual question is real.
The evidence should be examined.
And the undisputed Gospel of Jesus Christ remains worthy of our complete trust and obedience.
Now, there is another Greek expression worth remembering.
In John 8:11, the final command attributed to Jesus is:
μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε
mēketi hamartane.
“Sin no more,” or “Do not continue sinning.”
The expression is not permission to imagine that believers can attain sinless perfection through their own strength.
Nor should it be softened into a meaningless suggestion.
It is a call to leave sin behind.
And that call is consistent with the wider New Testament.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live godly lives.
Grace does not merely forgive.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
Grace brings us to Christ, and Christ changes the direction of our lives.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message is not simply that Jesus can make your past feel less painful.
It is that Jesus Christ can redeem sinners and give them new life.
Your scandal is not stronger than His grace.
Your shame is not beyond His mercy.
Your past is not a greater authority than the risen Savior.
But His grace is not an invitation to protect the very sin He came to save you from.
It is an invitation to repent.
To surrender.
To stop hiding.
To bring the truth into the light.
To trust the One who died for sinners and rose again.
Maybe you have been avoiding God because you believe He already knows too much about you.
He does know.
Psalm 139 reminds us that nothing about our lives is hidden from Him.
But the Gospel announces something astonishing.
The God who knows the truth about our sin has provided a Savior.
And you do not have to invent a better version of your past before coming to Christ.
You come confessing the truth.
You come with repentance and faith.
You come because Jesus saves sinners.
Not because you have finally become impressive enough to deserve Him.
If this article has exposed something in your heart, do not rush past it.
Maybe you have been more interested in proving someone wrong than helping them find Christ.
Maybe you have used religious knowledge to hide your own disobedience.
Maybe you have been quietly convinced that your past disqualifies you from ever being loved by God.
Or maybe you have been taught to fear every difficult question about the Bible, as though one manuscript footnote could destroy the risen Lord.
Hear this carefully.
Our confidence is not built on pretending every textual question has an easy answer.
Our confidence rests in Jesus Christ, whose death and resurrection are proclaimed throughout the New Testament.
And because He is worthy of our trust, we can pursue truth without panic.
We can acknowledge uncertainty without abandoning faith.
We can recognize the seriousness of sin without becoming cruel.
And we can proclaim grace without denying repentance.
That is the kind of discipleship Gospel Warrior exists to encourage.
Not shallow religious excitement that disappears tomorrow.
Not viral arguments that leave hearts unchanged.
But Scripture-centered growth that draws people closer to Jesus Christ.
If you have been searching for a Christian community that takes both biblical truth and personal transformation seriously, I want to invite you to walk with us.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible to people who are hungry for God's Word.
And there is a practical way you can help us continue and expand that mission.
It is a voluntary act of support for a ministry mission you believe is worth sustaining.
For those who choose to give from a heart of worship, that support may be understood as part of their Christian generosity and offering to God.
But let us keep this biblically clear.
Scripture says in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
But a meaningful opportunity to help sustain and expand Christian teaching and discipleship resources.
These items can serve as reminders of biblical truth, tools for reflection, or thoughtful gifts that encourage others in their walk with Christ.
It is the opportunity to help more people encounter Scripture, hear the Gospel, and grow as disciples of Jesus.
If that mission matters to you, we would be grateful to have you alongside us.
You never know who among your friends has been struggling with doubts about the Bible.
Someone may have encountered the brackets around John 7:53–8:11 and quietly wondered whether Scripture could still be trusted.
Someone may be carrying shame that has kept them away from prayer.
Someone may need to understand that God's grace does not excuse sin but calls us into a new life through Christ.
And someone may need to hear that difficult questions do not have to become the end of faith.
And please, do not leave without joining the conversation.
I want to ask you something personal.

When you read the story of the woman caught in adultery, do you identify more with the woman who needed mercy, the accusers who needed humility, or someone who is still struggling to understand how truth and grace belong together?
Comment honestly.
You can write, “Christ is still healing me,” if you know God is still working in your life.
Or comment, “I want to know His Word,” if this discussion has encouraged you to study Scripture more carefully.
If you need prayer, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.” You do not have to share private details to be welcomed into prayer.

And if you disagree with any of the textual conclusions presented here, you are welcome to explain your reasoning respectfully. Let us be people who love the truth enough to examine evidence and love one another enough to remain gracious.
Because the purpose of studying Scripture is not to win arguments while losing the character of Christ.
It is to know the Lord, understand His Word, and respond in faith and obedience.
Before you close this article, I want you to remember the original question.
Why do some modern Bibles place brackets around the story of the woman caught in adultery?
Because significant ancient manuscript evidence raises serious doubt that John 7:53–8:11 was part of the Gospel's original text.
That is the historically responsible answer.
But here is the greater truth.
No brackets can remove the mercy of Jesus from the undisputed pages of Scripture.
No manuscript debate can erase the cross.
No textual footnote can undo the resurrection.
And no uncertainty about this particular passage changes the Gospel's invitation to repent, believe in Christ, receive forgiveness, and walk in newness of life.
The Bible is not asking you to build your hope on the uncertain placement of one ancient story.
It is calling you to place your hope in the crucified and risen Savior.
So study carefully.
Ask difficult questions.
Reject sensational claims.
Tell the truth about the evidence.
And above all, come to Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest question is not whether a printer placed brackets around a passage.
It is whether you will allow the truth of God's Word to confront your sin and lead you to the Savior.
And perhaps the most haunting thing about this entire discussion is this:
You can spend your whole life arguing about the stones in someone else's hands while refusing to surrender the one you are holding.
